body_markdown:
The car looks just like the one from the poster in your childhood bedroom, except now that photo is in a for-sale ad rather than tucked into the rolling cases that appeared in the library during the school book fair. With money in the bank and space in the driveway, it’s finally time to make a dream into reality. Buying your first vintage car is exciting, and plenty of nerves go along with it. The excitement can make it tough to look at a new car with clear eyes and mind, so here are four things to stop and think about before wiring the money or hitching up the trailer.


## Letting “The Perfect Car” Get Away


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


A lot of us who are shopping for a vintage car are seeking out a *specific* car. Maybe not an exact VIN, but at least a certain model, trim, color, engine, or combination of options. I know I was when I started shopping for the 1965 Chevrolet Corvair that now sits in my garage. I had a checklist, which helped prevent me from becoming sidetracked and impulse-buying something that seemed great but would bring me regret by spring. (As regular readers know, I *never* impulse-buy vehicles.[Especially not broken ones.](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/mechanical-sympathy/i-bought-a-corvette-without-really-trying/) )


What I didn’t do was advertise that shopping list or be very specific about my wants with a prospective seller when I was looking at a given vehicle. Why? It has never been easier to convince an excited buyer that their dream car is sitting on a dealer lot right now, exactly as they want it, and all that’s needed is to send a deposit—or worse, payment in full—to make sure it doesn’t get away. Buying cars has a certain poker element to it, and while some buyers and sellers really ham that up, every buyer should at least be able to have a poker face. You will know when you’ve found the perfect car, but the person selling it doesn’t need to know that.


The point of this suggestion isn’t to encourage more aggressive negotiation. It’s more about protecting yourself from someone who might leverage your excitement to rush you into a deal prematurely. The vast majority of cars are not 1-of-1, and patience often reveals similar cars for sale in due time. Don’t settle, but be wary of getting caught up in the urgency of securing the “perfect” car and neglecting your due diligence.


## Trusting Appearances


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


A fresh, shiny coat of paint or an immaculate engine bay does not tell the whole story of a car. Neither is a bad thing, but it is common enough for a mediocre car to get a decent-looking paint job and no mechanical work and then be listed as “restored,” only for the next owner to find that the restoration is anything but complete, and they now have to do that additional work while trying not to damage a good paint job.


Every prospective vintage-car buyer has different wants and needs, so be honest with yourself about what work you’re willing to take on, and inspect a car accordingly. Museum restorations and cars with few miles after mountains of work should be assessed with extra care, and assumed to need more than you thought at first glance.


## “It Just Needs…”


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


When a car is described as “needing work,” that doesn’t always mean that it’s a project or two away from perfection. Case in point is the 1969 Austin Healey Sprite that I bought a few years back that was advertised as needing a brake flush and readjustment of the shifter.


As it turned out, the car *also* needed a new throw-out bearing, which required removing the engine and transmission from the car. I got a good-enough deal on the car, and was prepared to do such work myself, and was thus unbothered about it; but you may not be in the same situation.


Especially if a seller discloses problems with the car, it’s time to do your research. Know at least the common problems for the car you are shopping for and be sure to investigate other issues that you can assess during (or before) inspection. What sounds simple can quickly spiral into a nightmare when parts availability or pricing are different than expected.


## It’s Rare for a Reason


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


When starting out with vintage and classic cars, it’s fun to daydream about having a one-of-one or being the only one at the car show with a particular type or model. While that is fun, an uncommon car may require significantly more maintenance to enable the same set of fun weekend activities as a more common vintage car. That little blue Healey I mentioned above reinforced this lesson for me: It needed a lot of heavy-lift work, but the parts were easily available, plus knowledge and advice were just as easy to find. If I had bought a prewar car from a defunct manufacturer, I would have had a very different experience.


Playing with vintage cars is like learning to swim. Sure, some people have learned to swim by jumping off a boat a mile out at sea, but starting in the shallow end of a pool with a lifeguard on duty often leads to a better experience. Choosing a common and well-documented car or truck allows you to accumulate experience while enjoying the safety net of widespread knowledge. Your second, third, or fourth vintage car can slide a click or two further over on the scale toward weird and wonderful, as your experience with more common problems strengthens your ability to think critically when faced with fixes that aren’t straightforward.


You can’t eliminate every risk when shopping for a vintage car, but a little bit of preparation and critical thinking can significantly limit the chances of disaster. Have a tip for a first-time vintage car buyer that we didn’t cover here? Leave it as a comment down below.
